 Fireworks lit up adland on Dhanteras Eve
 WPP and Publicis Groupe have engaged in a public dispute regarding agency selection practices and pitch methodologies. Publicis challenged WPP's decisions, particularly regarding the Coca-Cola North American media review. Cindy Rose from WPP questioned agencies securing business without traditional pitches while emphasizing the need for due diligence. In contrast, Publicis defended its approach, stating that skipping pitches does not eliminate thorough evaluations.

 Highlights
 Publicis critiques WPP's 'CEO handshake' comments amid agency disputes.
 WPP skips Coca-Cola's North American media review, raising eyebrows.
 Publicis defends pitchless strategies, emphasizing rigorous evaluations.
 A debate over whether global advertisers are choosing agencies through boardroom handshakes or rigorous evaluations has escalated into a public spat between WPP and Publicis Groupe . Publicis has hit back at WPP chief executive Cindy Rose over her remarks on pitchless agency appointments, turning the spotlight on WPP's own decision to sit out Coca-Cola 's North American media review.
 In an open letter published on Instagram on November 6, Publicis called Rose's 'CEO handshake' remark an "insult to clients' intelligence" and questioned whether WPP's decision to skip the pitch was a matter of capacity or capability.
 Advt 
 The response follows comments made by Rose during WPP's third-quarter earnings call on October 29, when she questioned the growing practice of agencies winning major assignments without traditional pitches and stressed the importance of due diligence.
 The exchange comes amid a series of account movements involving the two holding companies, particularly around Coca-Cola and PepsiCo .
WPP's relationship with Coca-Cola dates back to 2021, when the beverage company established Open X with the holding company to manage its marketing operations. However, Publicis took over Coca-Cola's North American media in 2025 following a review, marking a significant shift in the relationship.
 The two groups were subsequently competing for Coca-Cola's global media business in 2026. But the contest took another turn in September, when PepsiCo appointed Publicis as its global media partner, moving the business from Omnicom's OMD after nearly three decades.
PepsiCo's annual global media spend is estimated at USD 1.9 billion. The company appointed Publicis as its global media partner, moving the business from Omnicom's OMD.
 Following the PepsiCo appointment, Publicis was reported to have withdrawn from Coca-Cola's ongoing global media review.
Coca-Cola announced the outcome of its review on October 22. WPP Open X retained the global media partnership, excluding North America, Japan and South Korea. Omnicom was appointed for North America, while Dentsu continued to handle Japan and South Korea. WPP also retained its global creative partnership with Coca-Cola.
 Advt 
 During WPP's earnings call a week later, Rose was asked why the company had not participated in Coca-Cola's North American media pitch.
Rose said WPP had already spent several weeks pitching for the business across other markets, including London, Shanghai and Mexico City, and had to prioritise delivering the mandates it had secured.
"We made a tough call between spending yet another six weeks pitching for North America versus delivering against what we had already won. It was a fine judgment call, which I made, and it is as simple as that, really," she said.
The discussion then turned to the growing number of agencies securing assignments without traditional competitive reviews.
 Advt 
 Rose then referred to what she described as the "CEO handshake thing" when discussing agencies securing assignments without conventional pitches.
Acknowledging that the cost and burden of traditional pitches were increasing, she questioned whether clients were adequately evaluating agencies before awarding major mandates.
She said, "These are really high-stakes decisions with material business consequences, and they deserve careful consideration."
"I do not think we do ourselves any favour as an industry of professionals by encouraging clients to bypass proper due diligence," Rose added.
Although Rose did not name Publicis, the comments came as the French holding company continued to secure major accounts without conventional competitive pitches.
 Advt 
 Publicis hits back 
In its response, Publicis argued that the absence of a traditional pitch did not mean the absence of a rigorous evaluation process.
"We all know global companies don't hand over their data, media, and tech keys over a friendly espresso," the letter said, adding that its appointments involved months of testing by marketers, engineers, data architects and procurement teams.
"Skipping an old-school pitch circus isn't skipping due diligence. It's clients knowing what they need and testing us to the limit," it added.
Publicis then turned its attention to WPP's decision not to participate in Coca-Cola's North American review, directly challenging Rose's explanation.
"You can't be a passionate defender of pitch culture and plead exhaustion in the same breath. If an extra six-week run was enough to sideline your teams, it's not an endurance problem; it's a capability one," the group wrote.
It also argued that enterprise clients were increasingly choosing agency partners based on connected identity and media solutions, intelligent creativity and AI capabilities.
Taking another swipe at WPP's handling of the Coca-Cola outcome, Publicis wrote, "A victory lap is fun even when you're the only one who ran."
The group added that celebrating a business win should not require undermining clients, agency teams or the work involved in securing mandates.
The letter signed off as "Your friends at Publicis". Its accompanying Instagram caption tagged WPP and read: "Hey @wpp, we're not angry, we're just disappointed."
